title: Sri Lanka strengthens UK business ties ahead of Expo 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:43
-     - {{hitsCtrl.values.hits}}

The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the Sri Lanka High Commission in the United Kingdom, conducted a two-day business outreach program in London on 21 and 22 October 2026 to promote Sri Lanka Expo 2027 and encourage greater participation by UK businesses.

The move featured a Business and Investment Forum and networking session on 21 October, followed by bilateral business meetings on 22 October. Around 140 participants, including British buyers, investors, representatives of chambers of commerce, business associations and trade promotion organisations, attended the forum to explore commercial partnerships and strengthen trade and investment ties between the two countries.

The initiative aimed to expand market opportunities for Sri Lankan exports, promote the country as a reliable sourcing destination and showcase investment prospects across key sectors. Sri Lanka Expo 2027 is scheduled to take place from 14-17 January 2027.

The Sri Lankan delegation was led by Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Cooperative Development Minister Wasantha Samarasinghe. Other members included Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry Secretary Thilaka Jayasundara, EDB Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe, and the Board of Investment of Sri Lanka (BOI) Executive Director.

Addressing the forum, Minister Samarasinghe highlighted Sri Lanka’s economic recovery, noting that the economy recorded growth of 5% in both 2024 and 2025.

He attributed the progress to the resilience of the Sri Lankan people, the determination of the business community and advances made under the country’s economic reform program. He also emphasised the Government’s continued efforts to improve the regulatory environment, streamline procedures, strengthen institutional coordination, and enhance transparency and efficiency in public service delivery.

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry Secretary Jayasundara, outlined the progress made in restoring economic stability and strengthening investor confidence. She noted that Sri Lanka recorded economic growth of 5%, while the industrial sector expanded by 7.8% in 2025. She also highlighted improvements in the country’s fiscal position, including a Budget deficit equivalent to 2.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a declining debt ratio.

Jayasundara further stated that foreign direct investment (FDI) exceeded $ 1 billion in 2025, representing an increase of 72%. These developments, she noted, demonstrated the opportunities available to investors seeking to establish or expand their presence in Sri Lanka.

Delivering the welcome address, High Commissioner of Sri Lanka to the UK Senadheera, highlighted the longstanding trade relationship between the two countries. He also drew attention to the opportunities available to Sri Lankan exporters under the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS), which provides preferential market access for eligible exports.

EDB Chairman Wijesinghe, outlined Sri Lanka’s export potential in the UK market, highlighting the strengths of the country’s products and services across key sectors. He emphasised Sri Lanka’s competitiveness as a sourcing destination, supported by sustainable manufacturing practices, authentic products and compliance with international quality standards.

He also delivered a detailed presentation on Sri Lanka Expo 2027, describing the event as an important platform for international buyers and investors to engage directly with Sri Lankan businesses across a wide range of sectors. He invited UK-based companies to participate in the Expo and explore sourcing, investment and partnership opportunities with Sri Lankan enterprises committed to international quality and sustainability standards.

A panel discussion on trade opportunities featured Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry Secretary Jayasundara, EDB Chairman Wijesinghe and Marks & Spencer (M&S) Head of Finance Head of Finance Suraj Wijendra. The discussion explored Sri Lanka’s potential as a responsible sourcing destination, its strategic advantages and opportunities to expand bilateral trade. Panellists also highlighted the Expo’s value for UK buyers seeking reliable suppliers and new business partnerships.

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry Secretary, Aistra Co-Founder and Managing Partner Eric Selvadurai, and the BOI Executive Director participated in a separate panel discussion examining investment opportunities in Sri Lanka. The discussion focused on Sri Lanka’s investment climate, emerging sectoral opportunities and potential for international collaboration. Participants were encouraged to attend the investment forum planned as part of Sri Lanka Expo 2027 to engage with Sri Lankan institutions and businesses.

Delivering the vote of thanks, Sri Lanka High Commission in the UK Minister (Commercial) and Coordinator of the Promotional Program P. Jayakody, invited the 140 participants at the Business and Investment Forum, including existing and prospective buyers, investors and representatives of business associations, to attend Sri Lanka Expo 2027.

Scheduled for 14–17 January 2027, Sri Lanka Expo 2027 is expected to provide a platform for Sri Lankan exporters, manufacturers, service providers and investment promotion agencies to connect with international markets and expand business opportunities.

title: Colombo Dockyard sustains turnaround with second consecutive profitable quarter | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:35
-     - 110

Colombo Dockyard PLC yestertday said that it continued its return to profitability during the second quarter of its 2026/27 financial year, recording its second consecutive profitable quarter and further strengthening the turnaround seen since the beginning of the current financial year.

For the three months ended 30 September 2026, profit attributable to shareholders reached Rs. 164.9 million, compared with a loss of Rs. 563.6 million during the corresponding quarter of the previous year. Earnings per share improved to Rs. 0.42 from a restated loss per share of Rs. 2.44.

The latest performance builds on the profit recorded during the first quarter ended 30 June 2026 and takes profit attributable to shareholders for the first six months of the financial year to Rs. 251.2 million. This compares with a loss of Rs. 1.37 billion during the corresponding six-month period last year.

The improvement reflects continued progress across several areas of the business, led by a strong performance from ship repairing, reduced losses from shipbuilding and a substantial reduction in finance costs following the Rights Issue and subsequent debt restructuring.

Group revenue for the quarter stood at Rs. 7.49 billion, marginally lower than the corresponding period last year. However, improved margins and better cost performance lifted gross profit by 53.4% to Rs. 1.56 billion, with the gross profit margin improving to 20.8% from 13.2%.

Ship repairing remained the strongest contributor to the Group’s performance. During the first six months, ship repair revenue increased by 32.4% to Rs. 8.85 billion, while gross profit from the segment increased to Rs. 3.28 billion from Rs. 1.87 billion in the corresponding period.

The shipbuilding business also showed encouraging progress despite lower revenue during the period. Shipbuilding revenue stood at Rs. 2.81 billion as recently contracted projects remain at early stages of execution. Importantly, the segment’s gross loss narrowed to Rs. 838.4 million from Rs. 1.31 billion a year earlier, following the completion of several legacy loss-making projects and the commencement of new projects secured more recently.

Net finance expenses for the September quarter declined by 40.7% to Rs. 294.5 million. The reduction reflects the impact of the Rights Issue and the restructuring of the company’s debt profile, which has helped ease the financing burden and establish a more sustainable capital structure.

Managing Director/CEO Thimira S. Godakumbura said: “The results for the second quarter are another important step in Colombo Dockyard’s recovery. We have now delivered two consecutive profitable quarters, supported by the strong performance of ship repair business, improved margins and a significant reduction in financing costs. The completion of legacy loss-making shipbuilding projects is also allowing us to move forward with a stronger portfolio of newly contracted work. These projects are still at an early stage of execution and therefore have not yet translated into significant shipbuilding revenue, but we believe they provide a stronger foundation for the periods ahead.”

The Group’s balance sheet also reflects the impact of the financial restructuring undertaken over the past year. Current assets stood at approximately Rs. 33.09 billion against current liabilities of Rs. 23.58 billion as at 30 September 2026, placing the Group’s current ratio at approximately 1.4 times.

Cash and cash equivalents increased to Rs. 17.27 billion. A substantial portion of this balance, approximately Rs. 15.46 billion, comprises interest-earning deposits held under lien as security for bank guarantees and other credit facilities supporting the company’s projects.

Debt restructuring has also changed the maturity profile of the Group’s borrowings, with a greater proportion moved from short-term to longer-term facilities. This has helped strengthen the Group’s liquidity position and provide greater financial flexibility for ongoing operations and new projects.

Administrative expenses increased during the period, reflecting the broader inflationary environment and its impact on operating costs. However, improved operational margins and lower financing expenses enabled the Group to maintain its positive earnings trajectory.

With two consecutive profitable quarters now recorded, Colombo Dockyard remains focused on maintaining the momentum of its ship repair operations, improving the performance of shipbuilding projects and strengthening financial discipline as it works towards sustained long-term profitability.

title: Cross River Bank partners Hatch as it expands internationally | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:11
-     - 63

Cross River Bank EVP and Chief AI Officer Pravesh Rijal in Colombo

Cross River, a global financial infrastructure platform founded by fintech pioneer Gilles Gade, has brought its global expansion efforts to Sri Lanka, with EVP and Chief AI Officer Pravesh Rijal visiting Colombo recently.

Rijal’s visit, facilitated by Hatch, one of Sri Lanka’s leading startup and innovation hubs, and its founder Jeevan Gnanam, included meetings with senior executives from several of the country’s major banks, the Fintech Forum, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, and the Presidential Secretariat. Discussions focused on enabling faster cross-border payments, expanding access to modern financial infrastructure for Sri Lankan businesses, and exploring how artificial intelligence is reshaping the movement of money and the future of financial services.

The visit marks a significant step in exploring opportunities to connect Sri Lanka’s financial ecosystem with global payment networks and next-generation financial technology. Cross River’s strategy centres on building regulated US dollar infrastructure that banks, fintech companies, and businesses worldwide can access to support international transactions and financial innovation. By connecting payment networks across currencies and markets, the platform aims to reduce friction in cross-border transactions while working alongside local financial institutions rather than replacing them.

Cross River already powers some of the world’s leading technology and fintech companies, including Stripe, X Money, Coinbase, Affirm, and Upgrade. The company pioneered embedded finance through a technology platform built on its own real-time banking core. Today, Cross River operates at the intersection of banking, fintech, artificial intelligence, and agentic commerce, as it continues to expand its global reach.

Hatch plays a central role in strengthening Sri Lanka’s startup ecosystem by connecting entrepreneurs with corporates, investors, development partners, and international markets. Through its incubation and acceleration programs, corporate innovation partnerships, and investment-readiness initiatives, Hatch supports startups in validating business models, accessing markets, attracting investment, scaling their solutions and continues to build pathways for Sri Lankan innovation to connect with global opportunities. Its role in facilitating Cross River’s visit reflects this broader mission of bringing international expertise, capital, and technology partnerships into Sri Lanka’s financial and innovation ecosystem.

The engagement opens the door for further dialogue on how global financial infrastructure can support Sri Lanka’s evolving digital economy, including opportunities for fintech innovation, cross-border commerce, and collaboration between international financial technology providers and local institutions.

As Cross River continues to expand into new markets, Sri Lanka presents an opportunity to explore how established financial infrastructure and emerging local innovation can work together to create more connected, accessible, and efficient financial services.

title: Sri Lanka Connect 2026 positions Sri Lanka as a strategic partner for Indonesian investment | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:05
-     - 56

The Board of Investment of Sri Lanka (BOI) participated in Sri Lanka Connect 2026, the Sri Lanka–Indonesia Business and Investment Forum organised by the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Jakarta on 16 October 2026 at the JW Marriott Hotel, Jakarta.

Convened under the theme “Bridging Markets, Unlocking Growth”, the forum was designed to strengthen economic cooperation between the two nations by fostering two-way investment, commercial and strategic partnerships, and policy dialogue. It offered policymakers, investment promotion agencies, business leaders, and investors from both countries a platform to exchange perspectives, showcase investment opportunities, and identify new avenues for collaboration.

The forum featured a keynote address by Indonesia›s Minister of Investment and Downstream Industry Rosan Roeslani and a video message from Sri Lanka›s Deputy Minister of Economic Development Nishantha Jayaweera.

Sri Lanka: the best business destination in Asia to grow your business

The opening panel presented Sri Lanka as a strategic investment destination in South Asia, highlighting its access to regional markets, advantageous geographical location and business-friendly investment environment.

Panelists at Connect 2026 Jakarta examined why Sri Lanka is an ideal destination for foreign direct investment, including government incentives and policy support, ease of doing business, opportunities within landmark national development projects, and Public-Private Partnership opportunities. Priority sectors showcased included: Real Estate Development; Logistics and Supply Chain; Maritime and Port-related Industries; Textile and Apparel and Pharmaceuticals and Healthcare Manufacturing.

The panel featured BOI Executive Director (Promotion) Ganga Palalkatiya, Colombo Port City Economic Commission Head of Branding and Communications Dhanya Gunawardana, Kalbe International Ltd., Director Rudy Santosa Irawan, and CBL Global Foods Chairperson/Group Managing Director and the Indonesia–Sri Lanka Business Council President Sheamalee Wickramasingha,. The session was moderated by Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Secretary General/CEO Shiran Fernando.

Sri Lanka as an investor in Indonesia

The second panel turned to Indonesia as one of Asia’s fastest-growing investment destinations, supported by strong economic fundamentals, a large consumer market, progressive investment reforms and significant downstream industrial development. Discussion covered the current status of Sri Lankan investment in Indonesia, the country’s evolving investment landscape, priority sectors for foreign investors, and institutional cooperation to further strengthen bilateral investment relations.

Panellists included Danantara Chief Economist/Managing Director Reza Siregar, Hayleys Aventura Managing Director Dr Wasaba Jayasekara, MAS Holdings’ Silueta Ltd., CEO Ruwan Keragala, and KADIN (Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry). The session was moderated by CIMA Global Learning Partner Akalangka De Zoysa.

The forum drew representatives of Indonesian conglomerates, chambers and business associations, Indonesian Government officials, Honorary Consuls of Sri Lanka and their delegations, representatives of Sri Lankan companies operating in Indonesia, media and social media influencers, and a Sri Lankan delegation including members of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce.   The BOI will continue to engage with Indonesian investors who expressed interest during the forum, in collaboration with the Embassy of Sri Lanka in Jakarta.

title: Investigation launched into tusker found dead with tusk removed | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:45
-     - 37

Investigations have been launched after a tusker was found dead with its left tusk cut off and removed in a forested area in Kahatagasdigiliya, the Department of Wildlife Conservation said.

Wildlife officers discovered the carcass on Sunday in a forested area adjoining a paddy field near the Kayagollewa tank, within the Meeminnawala Grama Niladhari Division. Officials believe the tusker died about a week before it was found.

Preliminary observations suggest the left tusk was cut off with a weapon after the animal’s death. The tusker is estimated to have been between 20 and 25 years old and about seven feet tall.

The circumstances of the death were expected to be reported to the Kahatagasdigiliya Magistrate’s Court yesterday, while the Pandulagama Wildlife Veterinary Unit will conduct a post-mortem examination to determine the cause of death.

The Kahatagasdigiliya Police, Army Intelligence and wildlife officials have begun investigations to identify and arrest those responsible for removing the tusk and to establish how the animal died. Wildlife officers and Civil Defence Force personnel have been deployed to protect the carcass.

title: Are Sri Lanka’s corporates ready  to meet rising shareholder activism? | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:05
-     - 52

In 2023, cloud software giant Salesforce became the target of a historic, multi-front campaign led by a swarm of high-profile activist investors, including Elliott Investment Management, ValueAct Capital, Starboard Value, Third Point, and Inclusive Capital. They cited Salesforce’s slowing revenue growth, bloated cost structure, and history of expensive, dilutive acquisitions like Slack and Tableau as the raison d’être for their actions. They demanded an immediate pivot from aggressive expansion to operational efficiency, margin expansion, and disciplined capital allocation.

Faced with escalating pressure and the threat of costly public proxy contests, CEO Marc Benioff and Salesforce’s leadership responded with swift corporate transformations. Salesforce initiated sweeping workforce reductions, cutting 10% of its staff and downsizing its real estate footprint to dramatically curb operating expenses. To demonstrate stronger corporate governance, the company refreshed its Board of directors, appointed ValueAct CEO Mason Morfit to the Board, and disbanded its dedicated strategic M&A committee to restrict further buyout sprees. Furthermore, Salesforce launched aggressive share buyback programs and eventually paid out its first-ever quarterly dividend, funneling billions of dollars directly back to shareholders. The collaborative restructuring paid off rapidly as Salesforce reported surging operating margins and robust free cash flow, driving a sharp rally in its share price. Satisfied with the swift operational pivot and improved financial performance, firms like Elliott withdrew their proposed Board slates. For me, this event stands as a textbook example of how concentrated activist pressure can rapidly force a tech giant to transition from a growth-at-all-cost mindset into a high-margin, disciplined profit engine.

Now a mainstream

Shareholder activism is now a mainstream, year-round force reshaping global corporate governance. Activist campaigns are surging, targeting companies across all sectors and size categories. No brand or market cap is too large to remain insulated from aggressive investor scrutiny. Driven by a desire to unlock shareholder value, institutional funds and boutique activist investors are increasingly using strategic leverage to demand immediate operational, governance, and financial transformation. 

At its core, shareholder activism exists on a delicate balance of risks and rewards. On the positive side, proponents argue that activist investors function as vital external catalysts for underperforming companies. By targeting bloated cost structures, stagnant management, or poor capital allocation, activists have succeeded in revitalising stagnant operations. These campaigns often force long-overdue corporate restructurings, accelerate beneficial M&A deals, improve Board diversity, and demand stricter executive accountability, generating substantial short-to-medium-term returns for shareholders. Conversely, critics contend that activism often prioritises short-term stock performance over sustainable, long-term strategic growth. They argue that pushing for immediate cash payouts, aggressive cost cuts, dividend hikes, or rapid asset breakups guts essential R&D budgets and erodes long-term institutional stability. Furthermore, public proxy fights divert tremendous time, capital, and leadership energy away from core business operations.

At its core, shareholder activism exists on a delicate balance of risks and rewards. Shareholder activism is now a mainstream, year-round force reshaping global corporate governance. Activist campaigns are surging, targeting companies across all sectors and size categories. Shareholder activism in Sri Lanka remains in a nascent, evolving stage compared to western markets

To survive and thrive in this climate, corporate Boards must stop being reactive. Modern executives must perform rigorous “activist” audits on their own operational portfolios, proactively engage in open, ongoing dialogue with top shareholders, and articulate clear, long-term value-creation narratives. 

Shareholder activism in Sri Lanka remains in a nascent, evolving stage compared to western markets. While aggressive institutional proxy battles and activist hedge fund campaigns are rare on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE), investor activism is increasingly manifesting through legal protections, regulatory interventions, and organised minority shareholder pressure. Historically, corporate ownership in Sri Lanka has been concentrated within family-owned conglomerates and tightly controlled voting blocs, which have often limited the power of retail and institutional minority investors to influence executive decisions or Board compositions. However, statutory frameworks, primarily the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007 and Securities and Exchange Commission governance directives, have empowered shareholders with mechanisms such as derivative actions, minority buyout rights, and legal remedies against oppression or unfair practices. 

Activism in Sri Lanka 

Activism in Sri Lanka currently centres on minority protections during mergers, capital restructurings, and transparency issues. Recently, minority shareholders of Associated Motor Finance PLC (AMF) pushed for minority safeguards during the company’s mandatory amalgamation into L B Finance PLC. After the company offered Rs. 55 per share to buy out minority investors and delist from the Colombo Stock Exchange, dissenting shareholders rejected the cash consideration as inadequate. Exercising statutory rights under Section 93 of the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007, minority investors formally demanded that the Board purchase their shares at a fair and reasonable value. Despite these objections, LB Finance finalised the merger, resulting in AMF’s share cancellation and license revocation. 

In early 2024, Japan’s SG Holdings Global announced plans to delist its Sri Lankan logistics subsidiary, Expolanka Holdings PLC, offering a voluntary buyout to minority shareholders at Rs. 185 per share. Minority shareholders mounted strong opposition, alleging that the exit price significantly undervalued Expolanka given its substantial global asset base, past earnings performance, and long-term potential. Activist retail investors characterised the transaction as an opportunistic buyout that disadvantaged local minority owners. The grievance led minority investors to file legal actions in court seeking to halt or reassess the offer terms. Following Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approval and the conclusion of the voluntary exit offer, SG Holdings increased its shareholding to over 99.6%. Expolanka officially completed its delisting from the Colombo Stock Exchange in September 2024. 

The above events underscore how Sri Lankan minority investors are leveraging statutory buyout mechanics and regulatory appeals to demand price fairness and transparency during corporate restructurings.

A common misconception about shareholder activism is that it targets broken or fundamentally bad businesses

Additionally, minority investors in Sri Lankan corporates frequently utilise judicial remedies under minority protection statutes to challenge majority decisions perceived as prejudicial. Courts have routinely seen applications for derivative actions and injunctions blocking major transactions or related-party transfers executed without proper shareholder consent or independent valuations. Retail investor activism also regularly flares during Annual General Meetings or through formal petitions to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Shareholders actively challenge Board decisions regarding delayed dividend distributions, executive remuneration, and inadequate disclosures on related-party transactions. As CSE listing rules evolve and institutional standards rise, shareholder activism in Sri Lanka is steadily shifting from passive resistance toward structured corporate governance accountability. 

A quiet reckoning 

A quiet reckoning approaches Sri Lankan Boardrooms. The days of treating capital as a passive commodity and Board seats as comfortable sanctuaries are coming to an end. For decades, legacy conglomerates and entrenched management teams have shielded underperforming asset bases behind voting blocs and historical prestige. But as economic pressures intensify and institutional oversight sharpens, corporate Sri Lanka must look inward and confront a hard truth: complacency is no longer an option.

When a company consistently fails to sweat its real estate, optimise its Balance Sheet, or unlock the true potential of its operations, it invites corporate predators and the sharp scrutiny of shareholder activism. Investors are waking up, recognising that persistent value gaps are not inevitable market conditions, but the direct result of operational inertia and unexamined strategy. Boards can no longer hide behind vague promises of long-term vision while current capital lies stagnant. To survive this impending shift, Sri Lankan Boards must undergo a soul-searching transformation. They must perform ruthless self-audits, adopt the mindset of an activist against their own inefficiencies, and prioritise genuine value creation over comfortable precedent. The market is opening, and accountability is demanding its seat at the table.

A common misconception about shareholder activism is that it targets broken or fundamentally bad businesses. Activist investors rarely seek out failing enterprises with structurally flawed business models or terminal decline. Instead, they hunt for high-quality, fundamentally sound companies that are severely underperforming their underlying asset base. Activists target the “value gap”, i.e., the discrepancy between a company’s current equity valuation and its full potential value if its operations and balance sheet are optimised. A firm possessing iconic brands, valuable intellectual property, prime real estate, or market-leading cash flows becomes an ideal target when hindered by bloated corporate overhead, inefficient capital allocation, or risk-averse management. Bad companies offer little margin of safety. Their deficient performance reflects terminal industry tailwinds or weak competitive moats. Conversely, an asset-rich but operationally sluggish company presents a lucrative canvas.

The days of treating capital as a passive commodity and board seats as comfortable sanctuaries are coming to an end. Sri Lankan boards must undergo a soul-searching transformation. They must perform ruthless self-audits, adopt the mindset of an activist against their own inefficiencies, and prioritise genuine value creation over comfortable precedent. The market is opening, and accountability is demanding its seat at the table

By acquiring a targeted stake, activists leverage structural balance sheet inefficiencies to demand divestitures, margin expansion, share buybacks, or strategic realignments. Activists do not arrive to perform medical resuscitation on dying corporations. They step in to unlock latent potential, serving as aggressive catalysts that force ‘lazy’ management to divest noncore assets, pursue carve-outs, and separate businesses they believe would be worth more on their own. As observed by McKinsey, the image of activism is not just about Board seats, buybacks, and proxy fights. Those issues remain relevant, but the activist agenda increasingly addresses operational and portfolio choices that influence performance and company value. Activists are signaling investor preferences for more-focused companies. They are pushing for CEO performance, Board composition, and management accountability, 

Be proactive 

In this light, there is a need for Sri Lanka’s corporates to be proactive in preparing for and managing the increasing involvement of activist shareholders. I suggest that Boards have a bi-annual agenda item to discuss governance, strategy, and operating issues which are likely to attract the attention of activists. Independent directors can be asked to think like activists and prepare a note for Board discussion. As observed by Peter Drucker; “The best way to predict the future is to create it.” Rather than treating activism as an unexpected crisis, forward-thinking directors can identify, up front, the key issues which are likely to create shareholder disappointment. By incorporating this review into the regular Board calendar, Boards can transform a reactive defense into a disciplined mechanism for continuous self-improvement and shareholder value creation.

Operationalising this bi-annual Board agenda requires a structured, three-step approach. The review begins with a comprehensive vulnerability assessment, where management and independent advisors evaluate the company strictly through an activist’s lens to identify weak points in performance, governance, or capital deployment. Next, the Board evaluates investor perception by reviewing feedback gathered from top institutional and major individual shareholders over the preceding six months. This step highlights any emerging gap between internal management expectations and external investor market views. Finally, the Board refreshes its activist response playbook, ensuring that communication protocols, media messaging, and advisory retainer agreements remain fully updated and ready for rapid execution.

During this bi-annual exercise, the Board must direct its focus toward five critical areas tailored to the Sri Lankan corporate landscape. The primary area of scrutiny is capital allocation. Activists frequently target companies holding excessive cash reserves or underutilised real estate earning sub-par yields. Boards must proactively justify these retained earnings against clear hurdle rates or return capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. A second critical focus is the conglomerate discount that often impacts Sri Lankan diversified entities. Complex crossholdings and non-core business segments can obscure underlying asset value, making it necessary for directors to conduct regular sum-of-the-parts valuation analyses and evaluate potential divestment or unbundling strategies.

Governance and Board composition represent a third key area of focus. Long director tenures, smacking of comfort zones, or a perceived lack of true Board independence invite significant activist pressure. Sri Lankan listed entities must continuously align their Board structures with updated regulatory frameworks, enforcing director refresh cycles and establishing strong independent oversight. Fourth, executive compensation must be scrutinised to ensure executive incentives are explicitly tied to long-term return on equity and total shareholder return rather than simple volume growth. Lastly, strategic communication and disclosure require attention. Opacity in corporate strategy and lagging reporting standards create information vacuums that activists exploit, making transparent communication essential.

To survive and thrive in this climate, corporate boards must stop being reactive. Modern executives must perform rigorous “activist” audits on their own operational portfolios, proactively engage in open, ongoing dialogue with top shareholders, and articulate clear, long-term value-creation narratives

Concrete outcomes 

To translate these focus areas into concrete outcomes, each bi-annual meeting must generate specific action items. The Board should mandate benchmarking of total shareholder return and price-to-book performance against domestic and regional peers over multi-year horizons. Independent perception audits must be conducted prior to these meetings to catch early signs of shareholder discontent. Additionally, directors should periodically conduct brief tabletop simulation exercises to assess response readiness across legal, regulatory, and public relations channels. By rigorously examining these core areas twice a year, Sri Lankan Boards can effectively eliminate the vulnerabilities that attract activist attention while building enduring trust with their shareholder base.

Companies spend way too much time trying to win fights against activist shareholders and not enough time asking a simpler question: What if the activists are right? Investors do not back companies to protect existing management structures or legacy strategies. They invest to earn a return that exceeds “risk free” plus “risk premium.” When activists appear, the response should not be to circle the wagons. Companies must objectively assess the thesis, adopt the ideas that make economic sense, and address the real underlying issues. When activist proposals fall short, i.e., quick payouts at the expense of long-term health, leadership should not just push back defensively. They must present a better, more compelling path to sustainable growth. When external critiques reveal legitimate operational weaknesses or financial drag, Boards must respond with swift corrective action. Preemption and preparedness are key. Open minds and a willingness to review are musts. 

Activism is expanding everywhere. It is on the rise. The best strategic move any Board or CEO can make today is simple. Conduct ruthless critiques of your own business regularly and fix the flaws before someone else points them out for you. Confronting investor pressure is not an exercise in defending the status quo. It is an opportunity to prove that leadership possesses a sharper, more effective roadmap for growth. Corporate leaders in Sri Lanka can no longer afford passive governance. Survival and success depend on preemptive self-evaluation: uncovering internal vulnerabilities, fixing systemic inefficiencies early, and clearly communicating why the current strategy remains the absolute best vehicle for sustained economic returns. Be braver in describing the future. Spend less time describing the past through boring annual reports. Start thinking like activists before they think about you.

(The author is currently a Leadership Coach, Mentor and Consultant and boasts over 50 years of experience in very senior positions in the corporate world – local and overseas. ww.ronniepeiris.com)

title: Real relief is engineered, not announced | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 04:01
-     - 39

Every month, salaried Sri Lankans see tax leave their payslip before they see their pay. For them, the debate on income tax relief is a question of whether the household budget balances after food, transport, school fees and loan instalments. The Government has indicated a proposal to raise the monthly tax-free threshold from Rs. 150,000 to Rs. 200,000 as revenue strengthens, with the timing and design still under discussion, and its stated medium-term policy is to lower tax rates while broadening the base and improving compliance. That intent is understandable and welcome. The real question is how relief is delivered.

Relief and the base must move together

The personal relief was raised from Rs. 1.2 million to Rs. 1.8 million from April 2025, and the first taxable band was widened from Rs. 500,000 to Rs. 1 million, with the 12% band removed. Some observers have reasonably cautioned that a further increase should be weighed against its revenue cost and the narrowness of the base. Those concerns deserve to be taken seriously, and they sharpen the case for careful design.

The base is narrow. Of the 2,547,322 employees in the Inland Revenue Department’s employer returns for 2024/25, about 75.6% had no tax deducted, which is consistent with earnings below the taxable threshold. On my earlier estimate, drawing on IRD and Labour Force Survey data, the system reliably reaches only around a quarter of the employed population. For 2024/25, only 25% of individual income tax returns were filed on time.

Between end-2024 and end-2025, registered income taxpayers rose 19% to about 1.3 million, and registered VAT payers rose from 21,227 to 33,187. The task now is to build on this by bringing the informal sector and self-employed into the net, and by keeping collections balanced between individuals and corporates. Relief that is not matched by a wider base leaves the same compliant taxpayers carrying the load, or leaves a gap that is filled later through higher consumption taxes that fall hardest on ordinary households.

The IRD’s APIT data for 2024/25 show how concentrated the load already is. Of the 2.55 million employees on employer returns, 1.92 million (75.6%) had no tax deducted. Their average gross pay was about Rs. 528,000 a year, or roughly Rs. 44,000 a month, which fits earnings below the threshold. The 622,419 on whom tax was deducted paid about Rs. 308,000 each on average. At the top, the 83,397 employees earning above Rs. 3.7 million (3.3% of the total) accounted for Rs. 150.5 billion, or 78.4% of all APIT, an average of about Rs. 1.8 million each. The table also shows how steeply the average tax rises between income ranges. It describes employees covered by completed employer returns for 2024/25, under the earlier Rs. 1.2 million relief, so it is a guide to the distribution of the load and not a basis for costing any change.

Individuals and corporates: how the balance looks

The balance between corporate and non-corporate taxpayers is the other side of the same question. The IRD’s 2025 data show that corporate taxpayers contributed Rs. 669.6 billion, or 59% of income tax collections, up from 57% in 2024. Non-corporate taxpayers contributed Rs. 461.7 billion, or 41%, down from 43%. Corporate collections grew by about 15% over the year, against about 4.5% for the non-corporate group. The corporate figure includes corporate income tax, dividend tax and remittance tax, while the non-corporate figure includes individual and partnership income tax, APIT , AIT and withholding taxes. The split is therefore by type of tax, not strictly by type of taxpayer.

Why the slabs, not the threshold, should be the key change

Raising the threshold takes everyone between Rs. 150,000 and Rs. 200,000 a month out of the net altogether. Revising the slabs delivers relief to those carrying the burden while keeping them inside the system. Today the first Rs. 1 million of taxable income is taxed at 6%, and the rate then jumps to 18%. An individual reaches the top rate of 36% at about Rs. 358,000 a month, which is hardly an extravagant income in today’s cost-of-living environment.

Consider, purely as an illustration and not as any official proposal, reinstating an intermediate 12% slab on the next Rs. 500,000, with the personal relief of Rs. 1.8 million unchanged. The rates would then run: 6% on the first Rs. 1 million, 12%, 18%, 24% and 30% on each successive Rs. 500,000, and 36% thereafter. The 36% rate would begin at Rs. 400,000 a month rather than Rs. 358,333. The effect on three illustrative earners is shown below.

The relief is largest in proportion for the Rs. 300,000 earner, who pays about a fifth less tax. For higher earners the benefit is capped at Rs. 10,000 a month, or Rs. 120,000 a year, so the cost per taxpayer is bounded. The total cost depends on how many taxpayers fall in each band, which the available IRD data, based on the earlier 2024/25 structure, cannot show. The Ministry of Finance and the IRD are best placed to compute and publish that figure preferably before the Budget. Importantly, nobody is removed from the net and everyone above Rs. 150,000 a month remains a taxpayer.

A package, not a single measure

This is an illustration of design, not a finished proposal. The final width and rates are for policymakers, who must weigh the revenue effect and the available fiscal space. The principles, however, are clear:

1. Pair any relief with a credible plan to widen the base, including the informal sector and the self-employed.

2. Keep the burden balanced between individuals and corporates, as it broadly is today, so that salaried earners do not become the default source of new revenue.

3. Deliver relief by reshaping the slabs, so that it reaches the middle and keeps taxpayers within the net.

4. Publish the revenue cost and the distribution of benefits alongside the Budget, so that the public can judge the fairness of the system as well as its yield.

Tax relief that reaches the common man should leave him better off and keep the system strong enough to serve him. A revised individual tax slab structure, alongside a wider base, can do both.

(The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity. Reference has been made to the Inland Revenue Department’s Annual Performance Report 2025)

title: Tourism must focus on value, not volume | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 03:57
-     - 16

Our tourism industry needs to reconsider how it measures success. For too long, the sector’s performance has been judged primarily by the number of international arrivals, with ambitious annual targets becoming the centrepiece of tourism policy. Yet, the latest figures offer a timely reminder that arrivals alone do not tell the full story,  and setting such arbitrary numbers just sets the stage for failure while the true story may be different.

According to Central Bank data, tourism earnings during the first nine months of 2026 declined by 9.2%, falling to $ 2.25 billion  from $ 2.47 billion during the corresponding period last year. International tourist arrivals also registered a marginal decline of 1.8%, with around 1.7 million visitors arriving during the period.

At this rate, the industry is unlikely to achieve its ambitious target of 2.6 million tourist arrivals for the year. But perhaps that should not be the principal concern. The more important question is why the country is earning less from the visitors it attracts.

A significant proportion of those entering Sri Lanka on foreign passports are former Sri Lankan nationals, who have migrated overseas and are returning to visit family and friends. While their contribution to the economy is undoubtedly valuable, their travel patterns and spending behaviour may differ considerably from those of conventional leisure tourists. Consequently, treating every arrival as an equivalent tourism success risks creating a misleading picture of the industry’s actual performance.

We must also recognise that its tourism product has a finite carrying capacity. More visitors do not necessarily translate into greater prosperity. Beyond a certain threshold, increased arrivals can place pressure on infrastructure, natural resources, cultural sites and the very experiences that make the country attractive. Sustainability must therefore be central to tourism planning.

The real challenge is to increase the economic value generated by each visitor. Greater diversification is essential. While promoting Sri Lanka in traditional Western markets remains important, India and other Asian markets deserve considerably greater attention. These markets offer geographical proximity, growing middle-class purchasing power and opportunities for repeat travel. More importantly, a stronger regional visitor base could provide a buffer when geopolitical developments disrupt travel from other parts of the world.

Connectivity must become a national priority. Better air links, increased flight frequencies and stronger regional connections can expand access to Sri Lanka, while encouraging higher-spending travellers to consider the country. Tourism promotion cannot succeed independently of an efficient aviation strategy.

The industry should also place greater emphasis on Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions (MICE) tourism, alongside high-end leisure travel. Business events, international conferences and corporate gatherings can generate substantial economic activity, 

while supporting hotels, restaurants, transport operators and other service providers. Similarly, attracting premium travellers, who stay longer and spend more can deliver greater returns without placing excessive pressure on destinations.

There is also a need for pragmatism when considering the country’s tourism offering. Sri Lanka should be willing to examine opportunities to attract high-spending visitors from South Asia, including through a more open discussion on regulated entertainment and gaming facilities. Rather than allowing historical sensitivities to prevent a policy debate, the Government should objectively assess the potential economic benefits, regulatory safeguards and reputational implications of such developments.

The next phase of tourism development must be guided by strategy rather than statistics. Sri Lanka does not necessarily need more tourists. It needs better-connected markets, higher-value visitors, diversified source countries and a tourism product capable of generating greater economic returns.

title: Experienced graduates,  yes — but never at the cost of rigour | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 03:55
-     - 32

When Nuwan Jayawardena asked me, as an academic, what I made of his views in “The expert shortage we are building”, published on 1 October (- https://www.ft.lk/columns/The-expert-shortage-we-are-building/4-798011), I did not need long to answer. I agree with him. He writes as a CFA charterholder and a practitioner who hires; I write after twenty years in the lecture hall, including my years as Head of the Department of Finance at USJ. We have arrived at the same place through different doors.

His central sentence deserves to be pinned on the noticeboard of every faculty in the country: universities must stop producing internship-ready graduates and start producing experienced ones. Yes. Firms that once spent years shaping graduates are no longer willing to, and AI is hastening that retreat. The cost of building judgment has been handed back to us. We can accept it or watch the senior pipeline he describes run dry.

But let me say plainly where my own conviction lies, because anyone who has sat in my classroom knows I have one. Academic programs are at a crossroads, and the way forward is not lighter theory but stronger theory, taught differently. The graduate the market now needs is more technical than ever and, at the same time, more firmly grounded than ever. Nuwan says it himself: a graduate without foundations does not become AI-leveraged. Access to knowledge is cheap. Understanding is not.

The students in front of us

No curriculum succeeds if it is designed for the student we used to have rather than the one sitting in front of us. Today’s Gen Z undergraduates are not prepared to learn passively, and I do not blame them. They have grown up with a device in hand, and long, uninterrupted concentration does not come easily. A two-hour lecture delivered to them is, quite simply, lost on many of them.

Employers often tell these young people lack emotional intelligence. I see it differently. They are not short of feeling; they are lost in too much information. Every answer is a search away, yet nobody has shown them which answers matter, or where their own future lies. They are less self-sufficient than earlier generations, not for want of ability, but because they have rarely had to find the path alone. What they need from us is guidance, and plenty of it.

That is precisely why Nuwan’s prescription persuades me. Real problems, mentors and defending one’s work under questioning are not only what employers want. They are exactly what this generation needs to find its footing.

Three pillars, climbing together

As an academic in Finance my proposal rests on three pillars, each developed across all four years:

Pillar 1 — Know Finance: financial knowledge and conceptual foundations.

Pillar 2 — Analyse, Build and Validate: financial analytics, technology and problem-solving.

Pillar 3 — Demonstrate Professional Judgment: industry practice, decision-making and professional accountability.

Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy — remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create — is the ladder that connects them. I am firm on one design choice: we do not assign one pillar to one rung, with theory at the bottom and practice at the top. That is the old model, where the university teaches and the employer finishes the job. All three pillars climb together, so judgment is practiced from the first year rather than discovered in the last.

At the top of the first pillar, a student critically assesses competing theories and brings them to bear on a problem she has never seen. At the top of the second, she designs an analytical solution, tests its assumptions and challenges AI outputs rather than accepting them. At the top of the third, she delivers an original solution to a real finance problem and defends it before people qualified to question her. That is the defensible judgment Nuwan rightly calls the most valuable capability of all.

Higher-order thinking is not saved for the final year. A first-year student can weigh two simple savings options; a final-year student evaluates an investment decision clouded by uncertain forecasts, model risk and regulation. The thinking is the same kind. Its complexity and its stakes rise.

Examining the person

Take a valuation project on a real listed company. Students apply what they know about financial statements, cash flows, discount rates and risk. They build a discounted cash flow model, run sensitivity analysis, compare it with market evidence and test any AI-generated assumptions. Then they recommend a valuation range, explain its uncertainty to an industry panel and defend it, individually, under questioning.

I do not mark them on whether the number is “right”. I mark them on whether they can explain it, test it and stand behind it. This is what Nuwan calls examining the person, not the artefact. When the artefact can be produced in seconds, it is the only assessment that still tells me what a graduate can really do.

A friendly word on rigour

Here I must be candid, as my students would expect of me. Nuwan proposes that 60 to 70 per cent of the final two years be spent on paid, real work. I share the aim, and his point that a paid student is properly supervised is well made. My caution concerns proportion, and I offer it for all of us to think about.

Things are changing radically, but that is no reason to set academic rigour aside; it is the very reason to hold on to it. The advanced theory of the final years is what allows a graduate to question a model’s assumptions. If too much of that time leaves the university, placement risks becoming a substitute for teaching rather than its culmination. A strong program should change with the times, yet its rigour should stand firm through every change. Integration, not displacement, serves both our aims.

Where our proposals meet

The three pillars give Nuwan’s ideas a natural home. His discovery phase fits first-year observation of industry. His problem briefs become the material of the second and third years. His paid, supervised work and defended outputs crown the fourth. I also share his reading of the quieter obstacles: industry supervision must count towards promotion as research does, placement brokerage should be professionally staffed, and practice-track appointments would add capacity without stretching existing staff.

The answer from the lecture hall

Where will the next expert come from? From the universities, as Nuwan says, but only if we change what a degree is. Not a timetable of content followed by the hope that industry will finish the job, but a deliberate journey in which students learn finance, use technology to test it, and learn to make and defend professional decisions, with a guiding hand beside them all the way.

To firms: bring us your problems, data and panels from the first year, not only placement slots in the last. To professional bodies: help us standardise what counts. To fellow academics: the three pillars are not an extra burden; they describe what good teaching was always meant to achieve. And to our students: we will guide you, but we will not lower the bar.

The teaching hospital, as Nuwan reminds us, has always known that judgment cannot be learned from a book. It has also always known that judgment cannot be built without one. Our degrees must now stand on both truths at once.

(The author is a Senior Lecturer and former Head of the Department of Finance, Faculty of Management Studies and Commerce, University of Sri Jayewardenepura. The views expressed are personal and AI tools were used in the drafting of this article)

title: Surplus that starves | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 3 November 2026 03:48
-     - 54

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his Government’s real test was never stabilisation

In September 2024, Sri Lanka handed the National People’s Power the cleanest mandate in its history. Two years on, the question is no longer whether the Government means well. It is whether it can deliver.

First, remember what was handed over. The NPP did not inherit a collapse; it inherited a recovery. In 2022, the economy had shrunk 7.3% and the country had defaulted on its foreign debt. By September 2024, under the IMF programme agreed in March 2023, growth was back to 5% in the first half of the year. Inflation stood at −0.5%, reserves had rebuilt to about $ 6 billion, and interest rates had been cut by 7.5 percentage points. Two days before the election, the outgoing Government reached an agreement in principle with international bondholders. The hardest part of the rescue was done. The test for the new Government was never stabilisation. It was what came next.

The new Government has built on that inheritance, and the record deserves credit. Growth held at 5% in 2025. Per capita income reached an all-time high of $ 5,003. Inflation stayed below zero for most of 2025. The stock market doubled from about 11,300 points at the election to 22,624 by December 2025. Tax revenue rose from 12.3% to 15.4% of GDP in a single year, and the primary surplus hit a record 5.4% of GDP. Government debt fell from 98.4% to 94.9% of GDP. These are real achievements, and any honest scorecard begins with them.

Year one was a good year for stability: low inflation, falling rates, record revenue and a booming market. Year two has reversed most of those gains, and the oil shock explains only part of it.

But look closer at how that surplus was made.

A Government that collects but does not build

A budget surplus is earned in two ways: by raising more or by spending less. This Government has done both, and the second is the problem.

In 2026, Parliament approved Rs. 1,380 billion for capital investment: the roads, hospitals, schools and water schemes that make an economy grow. By the end of September, about Rs. 385 billion had been spent. That is roughly 28% of the year’s investment budget, with three months left. The Finance Ministry says 70% of spending usually happens in November. If so, that is not a plan; it is a year-end rush in which quality is the first casualty.

The pattern runs through the line ministries. A Right to Information disclosure from July 2025 showed that only 19% of the Health Ministry’s Rs. 18 billion medicine allocation had been spent at mid-year. For new hospital buildings, the figure was 10%. Twenty-five health construction projects, some begun in 2014, still need Rs. 76 billion to finish.

Meanwhile, the money keeps coming in. In the first half of 2026, tax revenue rose 26%. The Government ran an overall budget surplus of Rs. 9.5 billion, against a deficit of Rs. 406 billion a year earlier. A country still rebuilding from Cyclone Ditwah, with hospitals unfinished and roads washed away, posted a surplus because it could not spend what Parliament had approved.

Taxation is not a growth strategy

Sri Lanka’s entire GDP, $ 108.8 billion in 2025, is less than two months of Walmart’s global sales. An economy this small cannot tax its way to prosperity. Growth must come from investment, exports and productivity.

The signals there are mixed at best. Foreign direct investment reached $ 1.06 billion in 2025, a genuine improvement. But in the first half of 2026 it slowed to about $ 450 million, against a full-year target of $ 1.5 billion. Exports did better: $ 17.25 billion of goods and services in 2025, and up 8% in the first half of 2026. Tourism tells a harder story. Arrivals hit a record 2.36 million in 2025, but earnings rose only 1.6%, so each visitor spent about 12% less. In 2026, arrivals are slightly down on last year.

A global shock, and who was ready for it

In fairness, the energy shock of 2026 was not made in Colombo. When the Strait of Hormuz closed, Brent crude peaked at $ 118 a barrel at the end of March, and every importing country paid more. In Europe the anger spilled onto the streets. Ireland saw fuel blockades in April. Since September, France has faced port blockades by fishermen and a revived Yellow Vest movement, with diesel above € 2.37 a litre.

North-East Asia stayed calm, and not by luck. Japan held about 254 days of oil reserves and released 80 million barrels in March. South Korea held about 208 days and capped pump prices for the first time in almost 30 years. China held about 120 days and Taiwan more than 100. They built their buffers in good years, for exactly this kind of bad one.

Sri Lanka had about six weeks of fuel. Within days, motorists were rationed to 15 litres a week, and from 16 March State offices, schools and universities moved to a four-day week. Sri Lanka has never built a strategic reserve, and that failure belongs to every Government, not this one alone. But it marks the difference between managing a crisis and preparing for one.

Preparing means scenario planning. Every year, a Government should ask what happens to fuel supply, the rupee and the Budget if oil reaches $ 100 or $ 130, or if the Gulf closes, and have the reserves, supply contracts and contingency funds ready before it does. Singapore has run a Government scenario-planning unit since 1991. Sri Lanka still plans for the year it hopes for, not the year it may get.

Interest rates and the rupee: The cushion thins

The stabilisation of 2025 has not survived its first serious test. The war in the Middle East sent fuel prices up 40%. Inflation rose from 2.2% in March to 8% by August. In May, the Central Bank raised its policy rate by a full percentage point to 8.75%. Treasury bill yields reached their highest level in 87 weeks. The rupee, at Rs. 310 to the dollar at the end of 2025, now trades around Rs. 332. The stock market has given back about 13% this year.

For borrowers, the turn has been sharp. Lending rates rose from 11.56% to 12.16%, and longer-dated Government Bonds now yield 12 to 12.5%. For a household with a pawning loan, or a small firm on an overdraft, that is the cost of living by another name. The rupee lost 7.2% in the first five months of the year and briefly touched Rs. 348 in the interbank market in May, before the Central Bank stepped in. A weaker rupee raises the price of every litre of fuel, every bag of fertiliser and every box of medicine the country imports.

Some of this is imported, and no Sri Lankan Government controls the price of oil. But a shock tests the buffers a Government has built. Reserves stand at $ 6.85 billion, barely above the $ 6.8 billion of December 2025, and short of the $ 8 billion promised to the IMF for year-end.

To its credit, the Central Bank has not printed money to fund the Government. Monetary discipline has held. Fiscal execution has not.

Slower growth, fewer jobs for the young

In June, the IMF cut its 2026 growth forecast for Sri Lanka to 3%, down from 4% before the Middle East war. The Government’s own target had been 5 to 6%.

Slower growth lands hardest on the young. An IMF comparison published in September found that 43% of Sri Lanka’s young people with post-secondary education are unemployed. That is the highest of 12 Asia-Pacific economies. National figures point the same way. Unemployment rose to 4% in the second quarter of 2026, and among 25- to 29-year-olds it jumped from 9.3% to 12.1% in a year. Net, the economy added only about 74,000 jobs over the year, while agriculture shed 174,000.

Hardship runs deeper than the headline poverty rate suggests. The World Bank puts monetary poverty at 16.9% in 2025. Yet in March, the Government’s own Rural Development Minister Upali Pannilage, said about one in four Sri Lankans lives in poverty. A 2025 survey by the International Food Policy Research Institute found that one in three households was moderately or severely food insecure, five times the 2019 level.

Families are borrowing to get by. Pawning advances rose from Rs. 660 billion in December 2024 to Rs. 1,012 billion by March 2026, up 53% in fifteen months. Credit card balances rose 17% over the same period, to Rs. 197 billion. Higher gold prices explain part of the pawning surge, but not why so many households are putting their jewellery on the counter. With State investment stalled and the 2027 capital budget cut, the jobs that would lift these families out are not being created.

Households: Spending on borrowed money, saving less

On the surface, households are spending again. Private consumption grew 9.1% in 2025 and 7.1% in real terms in the first quarter of 2026. But incomes have not caught up. At the end of 2025, real wages in the public sector were still 16.1% below their 2020 level, and in the informal private sector 11.8% below. The gap is being filled with credit. Private sector lending was growing 27% a year by April 2026, on top of the rise in pawning and card debt. Retailers now report shoppers buying only essentials, with inflation above 7%.

An economy is sustained by what its people save and invest, not by what they borrow to consume. Here the trend runs the wrong way. In its December 2025 review, the IMF projected national savings falling from 28.7% of GDP in 2024 to 23.2% in 2026, and national investment from 27.0% to 23.6%. The State saves by not spending its investment budget, while households borrow to stand still. That is not a recipe for growth.

Health: Allocated, not delivered

The health service shows the gap between allocation and delivery most painfully. The 2026 Budget gave Health and Mass Media Rs. 555 billion, its largest allocation yet. Yet medicine and equipment funds sat largely unspent at mid-year, and 25 hospital projects remain unfinished. Meanwhile, the specialists are leaving. The service needs 3,181 specialists and has 2,042, a gap of more than 1,100, and about 25 emigrate each year.

Agriculture: Going backwards

Agriculture shrank 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026, after growing 2.5% a year earlier. Rice production fell 15.1%, marine fishing 10.1% and tea 1.9%. In April, the Government had to allow emergency imports of Samba and Keeri Samba after the Maha harvest fell short. Farm employment fell by 174,000 in a year. Cyclone Ditwah destroyed an estimated $ 814 million of agricultural assets, and a bag of urea now costs Rs. 9,900 to Rs. 10,200. A country this fertile should not be importing its staple.

Energy: A promise reversed

Before the election, Anura Kumara Dissanayake promised to cut electricity bills by a third. Tariffs fell 20% in January 2025, then rose 15% in June 2025, well before any war. The Ceylon Electricity Board ended 2025 with a Rs. 38.7 billion loss. In February 2026, still before the Gulf erupted, it asked for a 13.56% increase, and from April tariffs rose by 8% to 14%. The war came on top, opening a Rs. 38 billion hole for mid-2026, which the regulator kept off 95% of consumers with a Rs. 15 billion subsidy. Low-quality coal, a procurement failure, cut output at Norochcholai. Most of the electricity problem was made at home. A third off was the promise, and voters remember it.

Losing money it already had

Good governance was the NPP’s founding promise. Yet between October 2025 and January 2026, $ 2.5 million meant for a debt repayment to Export Finance Australia was diverted to cybercriminals in ten separate transactions. It was Australia, not the Treasury, that noticed the money had not arrived. The parliamentary Committee on Public Finance found that payments continued after red flags were raised.

It was not an isolated failure. Around $ 625,000 meant for the United States Postal Service went astray through a phishing scheme, most of it in 2025. Two departments, the same weakness: payment systems that no one was watching.

Safety, and a disaster still waiting

Public safety has not improved. Police recorded 114 shootings and 60 deaths in 2025, more incidents than the 103 of 2024. By mid-September 2026, underworld-linked shootings had killed 17 people, including two children in a grenade attack in Dehiwala. The police service is short of about 40,000 officers.

Cyclone Ditwah, in November 2025, killed more than 600 people. The World Bank put direct damage at $ 4.1 billion, about 4% of GDP. Parliament approved over Rs. 500 billion for recovery projects. Nearly a year on, the opposition is still asking for a report on how much has been spent. The IMF’s latest mission called for removing the bottlenecks in capital spending to speed up reconstruction.

Power at the centre

The 2027 Appropriation Bill directs about 27% of spending to ministries held by the President, chiefly Finance and Defence. Previous presidents also held these portfolios, so the share alone is not the scandal. The trend in the President’s own office is harder to defend. Its allocation was Rs. 3.88 billion in 2023. It rose to Rs. 11.38 billion in 2026, the highest ever, and Rs. 11.2 billion is proposed for 2027. Meanwhile, the 2027 capital budget in the Appropriation Bill is 5.4% lower than this year’s, despite promises of Rs. 2 trillion in investment.

What has worked

The digital agenda deserves recognition. GovPay, the platform for paying Government charges online, has processed more than Rs. 5 billion across over 300 State institutions. Service charges on Government e-payments were scrapped in January 2026. The first digital identity cards are due by the end of this year. These are the foundations of a modern State, and they were built quietly and well.

The verdict: Country before politics

The NPP inherited a country on the road to recovery and kept it there through 2025. That counts. But a surplus built on unspent hospital and road budgets is not prudence. It is postponed development. When the first real shock arrived in 2026, the cushion proved thin.

If 2027 is to look better, the President must run the Government by delivery. Every key Ministry, from health and education to agriculture, energy and highways, should have three or four published targets for the year. Spending and progress against them should be reported in public, every month. Malaysia did this through PEMANDU, its delivery unit, from 2009; Britain did it through the Prime Minister’s Delivery Unit. Ministers who deliver should be backed. Those who do not should be moved, whatever their standing in the party.

That means spending the capital budget on time and in full. It means fixing the payment controls that let millions walk out of the Treasury, giving the families rebuilding after Ditwah an account of where the money went, and putting jobs for the young at the centre of the 2027 Budget.

The NPP promised a new way of governing. Collecting taxes was never the hard part. Building a country is. In 2027, it must be country before party.

(The author is a former COO of the Public-Private Partnership unit of the Finance Minister, an ex-banker and educationist)

What Budget 2027 should commit to

The 2027 Budget, due in November, is the moment to set the targets. Each one below can be measured, and each should be reported in public every month.
